Sardine Run 2017

By: Liz Fish | Production

Proposal


Show:

One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...):
The Sardine run is legendary off the KZN Coast line but for the last two years they have disappeared

Unique Selling Point:
Goolam Isaac has been a fisherman for the last 40 years. Each year he relies on netting huge catches of sardines supporting his family for months on what they made during the sardine run. His father did the same before him. But for the last two years there have been no sardines at all. This year they have had 3 days of fish, this week two more days. They spend the whole of July driving up and down the coast hoping those bait balls will come into shore. Often spending more money on petrol than what they make from the catch. Each fisherman has a boat and about 40 people that pull in the nets so a lot of people depend on those fish coming in.

Summary:
Sardines support a whole informal economy along the KZN Coast line. Buyers like Seggie Pillay tail the fishermen and haggle for the best prices. But when the fish don’t run they too are affected as are the families that buy straight from their bakkies. Sardines are a high source of protein that poor people depend on.
Sardines are a rapid growing fish, they spawn off the Agullus bank within a year of being born and then migrate along the coast of South Africa. But over the last 30 years their biomass has plummeted. Scientist are not entirely sure why. What they do know is that the ocean temperature is definitely warmer due to climate change and that narrow band of cold water has spread out and so the fish patterns have changed, they just aren’t coming inshore.
There has been massive over fishing 70 and 80s by Spanish trawlers off our coast line when the stocks collapsed. When that was curbed the fish stocks recovered somewhat but the ongoing over fishing off our own coast line by domestic commercial fisheries saw the West Coast sardines collapse. Those boats then moved around to Mossel bay. The Department of Trade and Industry has been slow to reduce the total allowable catch as peoples livelihoods depend on the sardines. In 2015 the total allowable catch was 950 000 ton and in 2017 it’s down to 23 964
There is a massive local and international market for sardines much of which is consumed by the pet industry. But it’s not only people that are dependent on Sardines they we are competing with Penguins and Gannets. They too are a casualty of the plummet in sardine stock. For example the Penguin population off Port Elizabeth has dropped from 80 000 to 4000. In the past WWF Sustainable Seafood guide had sardines on their Green list and this year after two years of intensive research they have been moved to the Orange list which means they should be eaten with caution.

Press Release:


Sardine Run
The sardine shoal migrating along the KZN coast was once described as the greatest on earth, resulting in
the legendary annual sardine run. But stocks have drastically plummeted and over the past two years,
fishermen have netted almost nothing. Carte Blanche asks: what’s happened to our sardines?

Script:


Script: Once describe as the greatest migration on earth the sardine run is legendary. Massive shoals migrate up the coast pursued by predators in a feeding frenzy. Every June and July for the last 57 years Goolam Essack has been gripped by sardine fever- he was 10 when he began fishing with his father
Goolam: Those days it was a lot of fever, plenty fish, big crowds, you can everyday fish you go any beach there was sardine now you have to look for the fish
Link: The sardine run used to be a major feature for all those living along the coastline of KZN around June and July silver waves of fish would wash ashore providing plenty for all
Goolam: last year was bad, no fish, the year before was no fish, year before no fish, 2015 we got a little bit of fish
Script: In June they had a few days of fish along the South Coast then nothing for a month then a few more at the end of July. Demetrios Stamatis was the only fisherman who caught a small net that morning
Demetrios: We were looking for a little purple patch and I was lucky enough to see it before anyone else this morning
Script: Once the fish are spotted its mayhem with everybody launching hoping that there are more shoals out there to be caught
Demetrios: We get about 12 baskets here it is a very small net but today lucky enough it is the only one so we will get some money from it
Link: Over the past few weeks these fishermen have travelled 100s of k’s looking for sardines and the question is are they spending more on their boats and crew than they are making from the sales of the fish
Goolam :for the last June or July I must have spent over I must have spent over R250 R300 and to make R200 000 to spend R300 000 you are not gaining you are still losing, see like today if you catch you are all right if you don’t catch there is nothing and you still have to pay wages
Script: The next morning they caught two nets and we saw the full extent of the fever
Goolam shouting
Script: As soon as the fish are netted the buyers move in haggling with the fishermen for the best price, Hawker Ryan Bolt says it’s a gamble
Ryan: We come down in the early hours of the morning 4am we leave home we wait we will sit sometimes they will catch fish in the afternoon about 1pm … 03 49 sometimes you can pay up to R1300 a basket and the next day R600 a basket R800 so it fluctuates so when you go back to the community the people want it cheap you understand so that the thrill of it’s
Script: It’s an intricate network of people. There are the spotters who have a particular skill in seeing the shoals, they alert the fishermen and then there is the posse of buyers who follow the catch
Goolam: I have got spotters all over from Port Edward right down to Richards Bay they phone me because like if you now if you phone me you get something from me
Kuben: It’s like a chain reaction you get a better price if you see the fish and if you call the guys to net it if you don’t you pay the price they are asking
Script: Spotter Kuben Pillay says when the fish are scarce it’s key that you are the first to spot them. His grandmother used to catch sardines in a rowing boat but now it’s an expensive and highly technical operation. Each year he leaves his permanent job to spot and hawk fish making 100% profit on what he pays for them
Link: We saw the crates of sardines been bought on the beach this is where they end up on the roadside and they have just about sold out.
Nareshnee: Its been difficult the last few years to actually get a good supply and it’s a bit late this year we expected it in June so we are quite happy to get it
Derek: What are the prices like?
Nareshnee: Oh the prices are a bit steep
Script: The great shoals kilometres long of Kuben and Goolam childhood are a distant memory and every fishermen has a theory as to where they have gone from changing currents to Chinese trawlers. We asked scientist Janet Coetzee what’s happened to the fish
Janet: These fish are characterised by boom and bust so typically their biomass remains at a very low level for 20 to 40 years even and then very quickly and drastically the biomass shoots up for a couple of years and just as quickly as it increased it decreases again
Script: Sardines have a short life span of 3 to 5 years spawning on the Agulhas Bank. The eggs are swept up the West coast by the current to nursery areas and migrate back to the Agulhas Bank by the end of their first year. But for several years now those young fish are not surviving - the numbers have plummeted and so the total allowable catch the TAC has been drastically cut.
Janet : The biomass peaked in 2002 at over 4.2 million tons currently we are down to 250 000 tons so about 6% of what the biomass was. Once the biomass drops below critical levels as it currently is then we bring the TAC down very quickly irrespective of what the socio economic consequences is and this is just to preserve the resource
Link: The small pelagic fishery industry of sardine and anchovy is the largest of all the fisheries in the country it’s a multi- billion rand industry. The sardine run only accounts for about 3% of the catch, the rest is caught offshore.
Script: In the boom of the 60’s the fish were caught off the West Coast and the bait and canning factories were built in places like St Helene Bay but since then the fish have moved to South coast. Desnice Ruiters works in the canning factory following in her mother and grandmothers footsteps.
Desnice “Everybody here is dependent on the fish there are 3 factories here that also pack fish and their people are also from here from the same place so from bad to worse
Script: Packers are paid by the hour when there are fish. They can spend months at home.
Link: There has been a 90 per cent drop in the quota over the last decade or so - and now it's down to 45 thousand tons. Normally its filled by this time of year but only 14000 tons has been caught so far – the situation is dire
Desnice it gets tougher every year because every year the quotas are getting cut …its difficult we can’t come out. You can’t fulfil the dreams of your children and you feel like you can’t give them anything and those children are dependent on you
Script: Johan Witbooi once a packer is now the HR manager and shareholder at West Point Fishing. With so little local fish they are importing frozen cutlets from Morocco to keep their 560 workers going.
Johan: We have a brand we must supply for because if we lose that market space then it will also have an impact on our employees but the other companies who don’t buy the Morocco cutlets you can see their employees are at home they are struggling
Script: 90% of the fish canned is imported frozen cutlets and with the poor exchange rate and increasing overheads they are struggling. Canned pilchards supplies the poor so the retail price hasn’t changed in 5 years.
Johan “If there is no work there is no pay for us and that is why we agreed with the Union to put in a one day relief fund at least to for the people to get up to R300 R400 per week to cover for weeks with no work
Link: But the smaller bait packing factories are totally dependent on the local catch and they can’t afford relief pay.
Script: Willem Walters company has two vessels but the quota is so small only one is operating putting 30 people out of work
Willem “When we are packing then we employ about 80 people. When we had 90 000 tons they could just survive but on 23 000 tons it’s impossible for them to survive.
Script: His packers have only worked 18 days this year
Willem “We are definitely not surviving at this stage. Our quota this year is so small and we bought quota in from other companies to make ourselves more viable, if we are going to catch all the fish that has been allocated to us.
Janet “So even if we had to stop fishing altogether now there is no guarantee that the stock would increase again. It’s a very complex process driven by environmental variability. You only need a few sardines spawning at the right place at the right time for the population to get a huge boost.
Script: And although the sardines arrived late this year- Goolam is hopeful
Goolam: In 2009 I think I had a run till December- in any case I say it might be a good run
